newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: FOCUS-Swiss National Bank acts to halt Sfranc rise.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Swiss National Bank acts to halt Sfranc rise.

text.p: The Swiss National Bank on Wednesday indicated it would continue to leave the monetary taps open rather than risk a stronger Swiss franc which could harm the country's slow climb back to economic growth.
Economists said this confirmed the SNB's current policy and oft-stated goal of keeping the franc from rising, rather than a break to a new, laxer monetary regime.
"I expected them to go ahead and put some liquidity in the market. The overnight fall in the dollar was too sharp," said Hans Kaufmann, economist at Bank Julius Baer.
The SNB's latest actions resembled its campaign last July and August when the franc also rose, and followed the mark's fall to fresh seven-month lows versus the franc Wednesday morning.
The mark rose back above 83.00 Swiss centimes, after it dipped earlier in the day to 82.39.
The dollar was also back on firmer ground, rising to around 1.4050 Swiss francs from a low of 1.3760.
Traders saw both the dollar and mark weakness tied to fundamental factors, leaving some puzzled at the wording of the SNB's statement Wednesday.

That statement said: "The SNB has said repeatedly that it would work against any unrealistic appreciation of the Swiss franc caused by developments in European currencies. In the most recent past, the upwards pressure lacked any fundamental basis. The SNB has thus reacted with a significant increase in liqudity. This policy will be consequently continued."
The SNB's 10-day reserves statement released Wednesday showed a high level of liquidity in the banking system.
Sight deposits, which along with notes in circulation comprise the SNB's M0 monetary aggregate, rose sharply by 724.7 million Swiss francs to 4.33 billion in the period to May 20.

The timing of its comments followed the news Tuesday that the U.S. Federal Open Market Committee left interest rates unchanged and it comes after a sharp drop in the mark after turbulence tied to European Economic and Monetary Union (EMU).

Kaufmann said Switzerland could hardly afford a too-strong Swiss franc. He said so far there had been no clear signs the Swiss economy bottomed out in the first quarter. Some economists question whether the Swiss franc is the main problem -- European trading partners' economies are also weak -- but they say the SNB cannot simply stand by and watch.

"The SNB must do something. Otherwise we won't stand a chance. I think the timing now for a strong Swiss franc is the worst that could happen to us. Now is the time that one books the hotels for summer holidays. We still are very dependent on tourism," Kaufmann said.
Michael Bernegger, currency analyst at CSFB in Zurich, has said repeatedly in the past that he expected the SNB to lower interest rates if the pressure on the Swiss franc increased.

CSFB analysts said Wednesday in a daily market comment that it was unclear whether the SNB's latest actions were sufficient to put a lid on the franc's gains longer-term, although they could "take away immediate downwards pressures on mark/Swiss and allow for a corrective recovery."
CSFB also said the traditional margin between the Swiss discount rate, at a historic low 1.00 percent since September, had been restored.
It remained an open question whether the SNB would, as it did last September, once again lower the Swiss discount rate, now at a historic low 1.00 percent.
The SNB does not officially target interest rates, but money supply.

Dealers said the SNB added liquidity Wednesday at slightly lower rates than those seen in recent weeks. One bank said it set a rate of 1-3/8 percent on a short-term operation this morning. CSFB also noted that the SNB did six-month swaps at 1.54 percent, "well below the bid side."
But some said it was too soon to say if the SNB had indeed eased.

"The problem is that the short market rates go up and down every day. The best thing usually is to wait. After a few days we will be able to see exactly what they have done," said Bernard Lambert, economist at Pictet & Cie.
